segments.title: Queen Mary as a triple-turret testbed
segments.summary: Martin Peacock proposes Queen Mary as a lower-risk testbed for triple turrets and oil firing than a battleship.
segments.question: Would Queen Mary have been a lower-risk testbed for triple turrets and oil firing than a battleship?
segments.answerShort: Possibly. Her speed and one-off battlecruiser role make the idea plausible, but the ship remains a counterfactual rather than a documented Royal Navy proposal.
segments.body: Martin Peacock's comment proposes Queen Mary as a lower-risk testbed for triple turrets and oil fuel than a battleship. The historical ship carried eight 13.5-inch guns in four twin mounts, reached about 28 knots, and had a maximum belt of nine inches and a range of roughly 5,610 nautical miles. That gives the counterfactual a concrete starting point. Three triple turrets could be placed all forward or in A, B, and X positions, while oil firing could support more speed or protection. The idea is plausible enough to guide further archival research, while the exact ship remains undocumented in this passage.

evidence.note: The speaker considers Queen Mary, oil firing, and triple turrets as a battlecruiser test case.

segments.title: Royal Navy test ships and the missing experiment
segments.summary: The Royal Navy's habit of testing major innovations raises an archival question: where is the oil-fired or triple-turret test ship before the Queen Elizabeth class?
segments.body: The Royal Navy often tested major innovations in a single ship before committing them to a class. An explicitly speculative 18-inch-gun test-ship theory is offered as an example of that institutional habit. If oil firing and triple turrets were active possibilities before the Queen Elizabeth class, the design sequence might contain a comparable experiment. A battlecruiser is a plausible place to look because it could combine speed, machinery, and armament in a one-off design. Documentary evidence would be needed to move the missing test ship beyond a hypothesis.

evidence.note: The speaker invokes the Royal Navy's test-ship habit and asks where an oil-fired or triple-turret experiment would have occurred.

segments.title: Designing a fast oil-fired battlecruiser
segments.summary: Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts tests whether a Queen Mary-like hull can reach 30 knots with oil firing and 14-inch triple turrets.
segments.body: Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts provides a rough design test for a British battlecruiser targeting 30 knots. The simulation substitutes 14-inch guns because it lacks the historical 13.5-inch option. Triple mounts, oil firing, geared turbines, auxiliary machinery, steering, torpedo protection, and armour are selected together. Their combined weight quickly determines which turret layouts remain possible. The simulation exposes the counterfactual's design pressures, but it cannot establish that a comparable Royal Navy proposal existed.

evidence.note: The simulated design selects a British battlecruiser, 30 knots, oil firing, and 14-inch triple turrets.

segments.title: Protection and displacement pressure
segments.summary: Armour thickness, deck protection, machinery, and turret layout rapidly consume the displacement available to a fast battlecruiser.
segments.body: The paper ship starts with a ten-inch main belt, five-inch deck armour, and a 30-knot ambition, then exceeds the 28,500-ton limit. A third triple turret makes the balance worse, so the simulation temporarily settles on two. Belt and deck thicknesses are reduced and the hull parameters adjusted until roughly 110 tons remain for secondary weapons. The sequence shows how quickly protection and machinery consume a battlecruiser's displacement. Triple turrets save deck space and some weight, but they do not erase the rest of the ship's costs.

evidence.note: Armour choices, displacement limits, and the effort to reduce an overweight design are discussed.

segments.title: Six guns versus the historical nine
segments.summary: The workable simulation carries six 14-inch guns, but a Royal Navy triple-turret design would probably seek a nine-gun broadside.
segments.body: After weight reductions, the simulation fits two 14-inch triple turrets, eighteen 4-inch guns with a twelve-gun broadside, torpedo tubes, and a 28-knot top speed. The six-gun arrangement looks balanced in the game, yet it underuses the central advantage of triple mounts. A Royal Navy design would probably add a third turret aft to reach nine main guns, then adjust armour or displacement to carry it. Secondary guns and torpedoes also consume the remaining margin. This remains a counterfactual judgment shaped by the game's hull and placement limits.

evidence.note: The speaker balances secondary guns and torpedoes, then contrasts the six-gun sketch with a likely three-turret design.

segments.title: Speed and firepower against heavy cruisers
segments.summary: A simulated fight against two slower Spanish heavy cruisers illustrates the battlecruiser aim of holding range while using superior speed and guns.
segments.body: The simulation tests the six-gun design against two Spanish heavy cruisers generated by the game. The displayed opponents appear to make 24 knots and carry four twin 9-inch mounts, 5-inch secondary guns, and guns reaching 13.3 kilometres. A 28-knot battlecruiser should be able to hold the range and limit their ability to damage it. The test ends in a win, although one 4-inch mount is disabled. These opponents do not represent an actual Spanish cruiser class. The tactical lesson is that speed and heavier guns must let a battlecruiser choose its range, while a third triple turret would strengthen the broadside.

evidence.note: The design is tested against two heavy cruisers, with the discussion emphasizing speed, range control, the missing third turret, and the result.

segments.title: Deck space and the value of triple turrets
segments.summary: Triple mounts can save turret and deck space, a particularly valuable advantage on a hull already crowded by machinery for high speed.
segments.body: Three triple turrets can provide more firepower than four twin mounts while using fewer turret positions and less deck space. Those savings matter especially in a battlecruiser, where the machinery needed for speed already dominates the design. The remaining hull still has to accommodate that machinery, protection, and secondary armament. Reducing the number of turret positions gives the designer more room to arrange those competing demands. The triple mount's value here comes from the balance it permits across the whole ship.

evidence.note: Triple turrets are presented as a source of weight and deck-space savings on a battlecruiser.

segments.title: Annual ordering and a possible experimental break
segments.summary: The Lion-to-Queen Mary construction sequence is used to ask whether the 1911 ship could have marked a deliberate experimental break in annual battlecruiser ordering.
segments.body: Royal Navy battlecruiser orders arrived at roughly annual intervals. Lion was laid down in September 1909, Princess Royal followed in 1910, and Queen Mary was laid down in March 1911 as an improved Lion. That cadence could have given designers an opening to try a different fuel or armament arrangement in the next ship. The dates identify where archival research might look for a one-off experiment, although they do not prove that one existed. This places the counterfactual within procurement timing rather than treating it as a blank-sheet design.

evidence.note: Lion, Princess Royal, and Queen Mary are placed in their lay-down sequence to suggest where a one-off experiment might fit.

segments.title: Oil firing and the Queen Mary boiler case
segments.summary: Queen Mary's 42 boilers become the basis for asking how oil firing might release space or power for a faster, differently armed battlecruiser.
segments.body: Queen Mary's 42 Yarrow boilers produced 75,000 shaft horsepower. In the comparison, the Queen Elizabeth class reaches comparable output with 24 oil-fired boilers. A Queen Mary-derived design using roughly 30 oil-fired boilers might therefore aim at 30 or 31 knots while freeing internal volume. Tiger's 39 mixed-firing water-tube boilers generated 85,000 shaft horsepower. The later Renown class retained 42 oil-fired boilers, delivered 112,000 shaft horsepower, and reached 32 knots. Oil could reduce the machinery count or turn the same boiler volume into much greater speed, so propulsion choices directly shaped the possible armament and hull layout.

evidence.note: Queen Mary, Queen Elizabeth, Tiger, and Renown are compared through boiler numbers, fuel, horsepower, and speed.

segments.title: One-off battlecruisers and design experimentation
segments.summary: The individual character of Queen Mary and Tiger makes battlecruisers a plausible place to look for a one-off design experiment.
segments.body: Queen Mary and Tiger are treated as closely related but individually distinct designs rather than members of a rigidly uniform series. Later battlecruisers continued the process of iteration. That pattern makes a one-off triple-turret and oil-firing experiment easier to imagine within the procurement sequence. A tightly standardized production run would offer less room for such a trial. Documentary evidence is still needed before this possibility can be treated as a historical design.

evidence.note: The speaker describes Queen Mary and Tiger as effectively one-off or iterative battlecruiser designs.

segments.title: Armstrong, Vickers, and British triple-turret evidence
segments.summary: Possible Armstrong and Vickers triple-turret designs lead to an archival question about what British firms actually built or proposed in the prewar period.
segments.body: Reports mentioned in the discussion identify definite 12-inch triple-turret work and possible 14-inch work by British firms. An Armstrong design associated with Italian requirements suggests that British engineers were working on triple mounts before the Royal Navy adopted them. A surviving photograph and later Armstrong information increase confidence that at least one example was constructed in the United Kingdom, although its date and exact form remain uncertain. Vickers involvement is inferred from industrial rivalry rather than directly established in this passage. The evidence supports an archival search for British-built models or turrets, while a specific Royal Navy ship design remains unproven.

evidence.note: British 12-inch and possible 14-inch triple-turret work, an Armstrong design associated with Italy, and the question of UK construction are discussed.

segments.title: Britain's competitive armaments ecosystem
segments.summary: Competition between Armstrong, Vickers, and specialist firms is contrasted with more concentrated German and Austro-Hungarian heavy-industry systems.
segments.body: Rivalry between Armstrong and Vickers makes it plausible that one firm's turret experiment would provoke a competing design from the other. Britain also supported specialist companies such as the Elswick Ordnance Company. This gave the Royal Navy several large or specialized sources of ordnance expertise. By contrast, the passage presents German heavy armament as dominated by Krupp and Austro-Hungarian production by Škoda, with neither company facing a domestic peer at comparable scale. The comparison is broad and qualitative, but it explains how contractor competition could generate technological options before the Royal Navy adopted them.

evidence.note: Armstrong-Vickers rivalry, specialist British firms, and comparisons with Krupp and Škoda are used to explain the Royal Navy's industrial advantage.

segments.title: Triple turrets and the prewar naval race
segments.summary: British twin-turret conservatism may have reflected a desire to avoid unnecessary escalation with Germany as the naval race widened into a technology contest.
segments.body: The lack of British triple turrets may require explanation as much as the technology itself. One suggested rationale is deterrence: Britain could match German twin-turret ships without escalating to an arrangement it did not need for superiority. The naval race may then have shifted from an Anglo-German construction contest toward technological competition among Britain, the United States, Italy, and Japan. South American orders complicate that picture because their battleships could be especially large and capable. This remains an interpretive question rather than a settled causal account.

evidence.note: The speaker weighs British twin-turret choices, German competition, and the wider naval technology race.

segments.title: Deterrence financing and the cost of war
segments.summary: The Royal Navy's large prewar budget frames deterrence as an insurance expense that may avoid the much greater costs and borrowing created by war.
segments.body: The cost argument compares peacetime deterrence with the much larger expense of war. Britain had the fiscal and industrial capacity to spend heavily on the Royal Navy when policy makers considered it necessary. A simplified example contrasts two pounds spent on deterrence with twelve pounds spent fighting, then extends the comparison across several days. War would probably require borrowing, leaving interest and repayment costs after the fighting ended. The numbers illustrate the logic rather than reproduce a historical budget. Saving on the peacetime fleet can leave the country with a far larger bill if deterrence fails.

evidence.note: Royal Navy resources and a simplified spending example are used to compare deterrence costs with war expenditure and borrowing.

segments.title: Presence, capability, and broadside superiority
segments.summary: Deterrence is divided into visible presence and paper capability, illustrated by a hypothetical British advantage in broadside weight and replacement capacity.
segments.body: Naval deterrence is divided into presence, meaning a force can reach and remain in a theater, and capability, its theoretical strength on paper. A schematic example gives a British battleship a twelve-gun broadside against an opponent's eight. Two British ships would therefore equal the broadside count of three opponents, while Britain's greater construction capacity would widen the advantage. Six such British ships would fire 72 shells in a broadside against 16 from two opposing ships. Britain could also absorb a loss more readily because five ships would remain. The comparison isolates broadside weight, fleet size, and replacement capacity to show how those advantages can influence an opponent before battle.

evidence.note: Presence and capability are distinguished before broadside weight, construction rate, and loss tolerance are compared.
